title: Der Zaunkönig und der Bär
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 102. Text from Wikisource („Der Zaunkönig und der Bär (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 102, an animal fable staged like a beast epic in miniature. A bear who calls a brood of young wrens dishonest — not fit to be royalty, he says, eyeing their shabby nest — touches off a war between every four-footed creature and everything that flies or creeps through the air. The fox, made general for the beasts, agrees to signal advance or retreat by the set of his tail; a spying gnat carries the secret to the wren, and the battle turns on a single hornet sent to sting the fox under the tail until his nerve, and his tail, both drop. The birds win, and the bear crawls off in real terror to beg the young wrens' pardon. Zaunkönig, literally “fence-king,” is the old German name for the wren — the bird of folk tradition who wins the title king of the birds by trickery rather than size, a joke this tale's title leans on without ever spelling it out.

sentences.t: Zur Sommerszeit giengen einmal der Bär und der Wolf im Wald spazieren,
sentences.l: At summer-time went once the bear and the wolf walking in the forest,
sentences.i: In the summertime the bear and the wolf once went walking in the forest,
sentences.n: “Zur Sommerszeit” — at the time of summer. “giengen … spazieren” is the separable “spazieren gehen”, to go for a walk, with its two halves standing apart; “gieng/giengen” is the 1857 spelling of ging/gingen.

sentences.t: da hörte der Bär so schönen Gesang von einem Vogel, und sprach „Bruder Wolf, was ist das für ein Vogel, der so schön singt?“
sentences.l: then heard the bear such beautiful song from a bird, and said “Brother Wolf, what is that for a bird, that sings so beautifully?”
sentences.i: then the bear heard such beautiful singing from a bird, and said, “Brother Wolf, what sort of bird is that, that sings so beautifully?”
sentences.n: “was ist das für ein …” is the standing German question “what sort of … is that”; the “für” has nothing to do with “for”. “da” opening a clause means “then, thereupon” and pushes the verb in front of its subject.

sentences.t: „Das ist der König der Vögel,“ sagte der Wolf, „vor dem müssen wir uns neigen;“
sentences.l: “That is the king of the birds,” said the wolf, “before him must we bow ourselves;”
sentences.i: “That is the king of the birds,” said the wolf; “before him we must bow.”
sentences.n: “vor dem” — before him: the demonstrative “der” standing in for a pronoun after a preposition. “sich neigen” is to bow, to incline oneself.

sentences.t: es war aber der Zaunkönig.
sentences.l: it was however the wren.
sentences.i: but it was only the wren.
sentences.n: “Zaunkönig” is literally “fence-king”, the German name for the wren, and the whole tale turns on taking that name at its word. “aber” in second position is “but, however”.

sentences.t: „Wenn das ist,“ sagte der Bär, „so möcht ich auch gerne seinen königlichen Palast sehen, komm und führe mich hin.“
sentences.l: “If that is [so],” said the bear, “then would I gladly see his royal palace too, come and lead me thither.”
sentences.i: “If that is so,” said the bear, “then I should very much like to see his royal palace as well; come and take me there.”
sentences.n: “Wenn das ist” breaks off short — “if that is [the case]”; the bracketed word is ours, supplied so the English can stand, since the German simply stops. “möcht” is clipped “möchte”, and with “gerne” gives “would like to”.

sentences.t: „Das geht nicht so, wie du meinst,“ sprach der Wolf, „du mußt warten bis die Frau Königin kommt.“
sentences.l: “That does not go so, as you think,” spoke the wolf, “you must wait until the lady queen comes.”
sentences.i: “It does not go the way you imagine,” said the wolf; “you must wait until the queen comes.”
sentences.n: “Frau Königin” — “Frau” before a title is a courtesy form, like “my lady”; the tale keeps up a whole court etiquette for two nesting birds. “mußt” is the 1857 spelling of musst.

sentences.t: Bald darauf kam die Frau Königin, und hatte Futter im Schnabel, und der Herr König auch, und wollten ihre Jungen ätzen.
sentences.l: Soon thereupon came the lady queen, and had feed in her beak, and the lord king too, and they wanted to feed their young.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards the queen came with food in her beak, and the king likewise, and they meant to feed their young.
sentences.n: “ätzen” is the old word for a bird feeding its nestlings (modern atzen or füttern) — not the modern “ätzen”, to etch or corrode.

sentences.t: Der Bär wäre gerne nun gleich hinterdrein gegangen, aber der Wolf hielt ihn am Ermel und sagte „nein, du mußt warten bis Herr und Frau Königin wieder fort sind.“
sentences.l: The bear would gladly have gone straight after them now, but the wolf held him by the sleeve and said “no, you must wait until lord and lady queen are away again.”
sentences.i: The bear would have liked to go straight in after them, but the wolf held him by the sleeve and said, “No, you must wait until the king and queen are gone again.”
sentences.n: “Ermel” is the 1857 spelling of “Ärmel”, sleeve — a bear with sleeves is the tale’s quiet joke. “wäre … gegangen” is the past subjunctive: would have gone.

sentences.t: Also nahmen sie das Loch in Acht, wo das Nest stand, und trabten wieder ab.
sentences.l: So they took the hole into heed, where the nest stood, and trotted off again.
sentences.i: So they marked the hole where the nest was, and trotted off again.
sentences.n: “in Acht nehmen” — to take note of, keep an eye on; the noun stands well away from its verb, as fixed phrases do in German. “kehren” with “um” is umkehren, to turn back, and the particle comes back at 16.

sentences.t: Der Bär aber hatte keine Ruhe, wollte den königlichen Palast sehen, und gieng nach einer kurzen Weile wieder vor.
sentences.l: The bear however had no rest, wanted to see the royal palace, and went after a short while forward again.
sentences.i: But the bear had no peace; he wanted to see the royal palace, and after a short while he went up to it again.
sentences.n: “wieder vor gehen” — to go forward, go up there again, with the particle “vor” left at the end. “keine Ruhe haben” — to have no peace.

sentences.t: Da waren König und Königin richtig ausgeflogen:
sentences.l: Then had king and queen sure enough flown out:
sentences.i: This time the king and queen had indeed flown off:
sentences.n: “richtig” here means “sure enough, indeed”, not “correctly”. “ausfliegen” is said of birds leaving the nest.

sentences.t: er guckte hinein und sah fünf oder sechs Junge, die lagen darin.
sentences.l: he peeped in and saw five or six young ones, they lay in it.
sentences.i: he peeped in and saw five or six young ones lying inside.
sentences.n: “die lagen darin” is a loose continuation rather than a tight relative clause — the German simply adds “they lay in there”.

sentences.t: „Ist das der königliche Palast!“ rief der Bär, „das ist ein erbärmlicher Palast!
sentences.l: “Is that the royal palace!” cried the bear, “that is a wretched palace!
sentences.i: “So this is the royal palace!” cried the bear. “A miserable palace it is!
sentences.n: The question form with an exclamation mark is scorn, not enquiry. “erbärmlich” — pitiful, wretched.

sentences.t: ihr seid auch keine Königskinder, ihr seid unehrliche Kinder.“
sentences.l: you are also no king’s-children, you are dishonourable children.”
sentences.i: and you are no king’s children either — you are base-born children.”
sentences.n: “unehrlich” in older usage is a matter of law and standing, not of lying: born out of wedlock, or from a trade that carried disgrace. That is why the young wrens answer that their parents are “ehrliche Leute”.

sentences.t: Wie das die jungen Zaunkönige hörten, wurden sie gewaltig bös, und schrien „nein, das sind wir nicht, unsere Eltern sind ehrliche Leute;
sentences.l: When the young wrens heard that, they became mightily angry, and shrieked “no, that we are not, our parents are honourable people;
sentences.i: When the young wrens heard that they grew mightily angry, and shrieked, “No, that we are not; our parents are honest folk;
sentences.n: “Wie” at the head of a clause means “when, as”, never “how”. “bös” here is angry, not wicked. “das sind wir nicht” puts the object first — literally “that we are not”.

sentences.t: Bär, das soll ausgemacht werden mit dir.“
sentences.l: Bear, that shall be settled out with you.”
sentences.i: Bear, this shall be settled with you.”
sentences.n: “ausmachen” — to settle, to have out; the word runs through the whole tale as the term for the quarrel and for its ending. The verb is “ausmachen”, to settle a matter — not the everyday modern “ausmachen”, to put a light out.

sentences.t: Dem Bär und dem Wolf ward angst, sie kehrten um und setzten sich in ihre Höhlen.
sentences.l: To the bear and to the wolf [it] became anxious, they turned about and set themselves in their dens.
sentences.i: The bear and the wolf grew frightened; they turned back and settled into their dens.
sentences.n: “Dem Bär … ward angst” is impersonal: fear happens *to* someone, who stands in the dative and is not the subject at all. The German has no subject at all; the bracketed “it” is ours, supplied because English cannot do without one. “ward” is the old preterite of “werden”.

sentences.t: Die jungen Zaunkönige aber schrien und lärmten fort,
sentences.l: The young wrens however shrieked and made a din on,
sentences.i: But the young wrens went on shrieking and making a din,
sentences.n: “fort” after a verb means to keep on doing it — “fortschreien”, to go on screaming.

sentences.t: und als ihre Eltern wieder Futter brachten, sagten sie „wir rühren kein Fliegenbeinchen an, und sollten wir verhungern, bis ihr erst ausgemacht habt ob wir ehrliche Kinder sind oder nicht:
sentences.l: and when their parents brought feed again, they said “we touch not a little fly’s-leg, and should we starve, until you have first settled whether we are honourable children or not:
sentences.i: and when their parents brought food again they said, “We will not touch so much as a fly’s leg, even if we should starve, until you have settled whether we are honest children or not:
sentences.n: “und sollten wir verhungern” is a concession made by putting the verb first — “even if we should starve”. “anrühren” is separable: “rühren … an”.

sentences.t: der Bär ist da gewesen, und hat uns gescholten.“
sentences.l: the bear has been there, and has scolded us.”
sentences.i: the bear has been here, and has reviled us.”
sentences.n: “schelten” — to scold, revile; stronger than modern “schimpfen”, and here it amounts to slander.

sentences.t: Da sagte der alte König „seid nur ruhig, das soll ausgemacht werden.“
sentences.l: Then said the old king “be only calm, that shall be settled.”
sentences.i: Then the old king said, “Be easy; it shall be settled.”
sentences.n: “nur” in a command softens rather than restricts: just be calm.

sentences.t: Flog darauf mit der Frau Königin dem Bären vor seine Höhle und rief hinein „alter Brummbär warum hast du meine Kinder gescholten?
sentences.l: Flew thereupon with the lady queen [to] the bear before his cave and called in “old growl-bear, why have you scolded my children?
sentences.i: Thereupon he flew with the queen to the bear’s cave and called in, “Old growl-bear, why have you reviled my children?
sentences.n: The sentence begins with its verb and no subject — the king is carried over from the sentence before. The bear stands in a bare dative (“dem Bären”) picked up by “vor seine Höhle”, before his cave: a dative of possession, the bear’s own cave. The bracketed “to” is ours, supplied so the English can carry that dative. “Brummbär” is a growl-bear, the name for a grumbling, growling creature.

sentences.t: das soll dir übel bekommen, das wollen wir in einem blutigen Krieg ausmachen.“
sentences.l: that shall agree with you ill, that will we settle in a bloody war.”
sentences.i: you shall pay dearly for it; we will settle this in a bloody war.”
sentences.n: “übel bekommen” is what bad food does to a person — it disagrees with them; as a threat it means “it will go badly for you”.

sentences.t: Also war dem Bären der Krieg angekündigt, und ward alles vierfüßige Gethier berufen, Ochs, Esel, Rind, Hirsch, Reh, und was die Erde sonst alles trägt.
sentences.l: So was to the bear the war announced, and was all four-footed beast-kind summoned, ox, ass, cattle, stag, roe deer, and whatever else the earth bears.
sentences.i: So war was declared on the bear, and every four-footed beast was summoned — ox, ass, cattle, stag, roe deer, and whatever else the earth carries.
sentences.n: “Gethier” (modern Getier) is a collective: the beasts taken together. Two passives run in a row on “ward”, the old preterite of werden.

sentences.t: Der Zaunkönig aber berief alles was in der Luft fliegt;
sentences.l: The wren however summoned everything that flies in the air;
sentences.i: The wren for his part summoned everything that flies in the air;
sentences.n: “berufen” in its older sense, to call up, summon (modern usage prefers einberufen).

sentences.t: nicht allein die Vögel groß und klein, sondern auch die Mücken, Hornissen, Bienen und Fliegen mußten herbei.
sentences.l: not alone the birds great and small, but also the gnats, hornets, bees and flies had to [come] here.
sentences.i: not only the birds great and small — the gnats, hornets, bees and flies had to come too.
sentences.n: “mußten herbei” leaves the verb of motion out altogether: had to [come] this way. German lets a modal stand with a bare direction; the bracket is ours, supplying what English needs.

sentences.t: Als nun die Zeit kam, wo der Krieg angehen sollte, da schickte der Zaunkönig Kundschafter aus, wer der kommandierende General des Feindes wäre.
sentences.l: When now the time came, when the war was to begin, then sent the wren scouts out, [to learn] who the commanding general of the enemy was.
sentences.i: When the time came for the war to begin, the wren sent out scouts to learn who the enemy’s commanding general was.
sentences.n: “wo” here means “when”, of time — common in older German. The bracketed words are ours: the German runs the indirect question straight onto “schickte … aus”. “wäre” is subjunctive because the question is reported.

sentences.t: Die Mücke war die listigste von allen, schwärmte im Wald, wo der Feind sich versammelte,
sentences.l: The gnat was the craftiest of all, swarmed in the forest, where the enemy was gathering,
sentences.i: The gnat was the craftiest of all; she darted about the forest where the enemy was assembling,
sentences.n: “die Mücke” is feminine, so German says “she”. “schwärmen” of insects: to swarm, to dart about.

sentences.t: und setzte sich endlich unter ein Blatt auf den Baum, wo die Parole ausgegeben wurde.
sentences.l: and set herself at last under a leaf on the tree, where the watchword was given out.
sentences.i: and settled at last under a leaf on the tree where the password was being issued.
sentences.n: “Parole” is the military watchword given out to the troops — not “parole” in the English legal sense. “sich setzen” — to set oneself down, to alight.

sentences.t: Da stand der Bär, rief den Fuchs vor sich und sprach „Fuchs, du bist der schlauste unter allem Gethier, du sollst General sein, und uns anführen.“
sentences.l: There stood the bear, called the fox before himself and spoke “Fox, you are the slyest among all beast-kind, you shall be general, and lead us.”
sentences.i: There stood the bear; he called the fox before him and said, “Fox, you are the slyest of all the beasts; you shall be general and lead us.”
sentences.n: “anführen” — to lead, to command (separable: führt an). “sollst” here appoints rather than obliges: you are to be.

sentences.t: „Gut,“ sagte der Fuchs, „aber was für Zeichen wollen wir verabreden?“
sentences.l: “Good,” said the fox, “but what for signs shall we agree on?”
sentences.i: “Good,” said the fox, “but what signals shall we agree on?”
sentences.n: “was für” once more — what sort of. “verabreden” — to arrange, to settle beforehand.

sentences.t: Niemand wußte es.
sentences.l: Nobody knew it.
sentences.n: “wußte” is the 1857 spelling of wusste, from “wissen”, to know a thing as a fact.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Fuchs „ich habe einen schönen langen buschigen Schwanz, der sieht aus fast wie ein rother Federbusch;
sentences.l: Then spoke the fox “I have a fine long bushy tail, it looks almost like a red plume;
sentences.i: Then the fox said, “I have a fine long bushy tail that looks almost like a red plume of feathers;
sentences.n: “Federbusch” is a bunch of feathers, the plume on a helmet — the fox describes himself as a piece of military finery. “rother” is the 1857 spelling of roter.

sentences.t: wenn ich den Schwanz in die Höhe halte, so geht die Sache gut, und ihr müßt darauf los marschieren;
sentences.l: if I hold the tail up in the height, then the thing goes well, and you must march right at it;
sentences.i: if I hold my tail up in the air, the business is going well, and you must march straight at them;
sentences.n: “darauf los” — straight at it; “losmarschieren” is separable and its particle “los” stands here in front of the verb. “die Sache geht gut” — matters are going well.

sentences.t: laß ich ihn aber herunterhängen, so lauft was ihr könnt.“
sentences.l: let I it however hang down, then run what you can.”
sentences.i: but if I let it hang down, then run for all you are worth.”
sentences.n: A verb-first clause makes a condition without “wenn”: “laß ich ihn” = if I let it. “lauft was ihr könnt” — run [as fast as] you can.

sentences.t: Als die Mücke das gehört hatte, flog sie wieder heim und verrieth dem Zaunkönig alles haarklein.
sentences.l: When the gnat had heard that, flew she home again and betrayed to the wren everything hair-small.
sentences.i: When the gnat had heard this she flew home again and reported the whole thing to the wren down to the last detail.
sentences.n: “haarklein” — hair-small, that is, in the finest detail. “verrieth” (modern verriet) is “verraten”, to give away, disclose.

sentences.t: Als der Tag anbrach, wo die Schlacht sollte geliefert werden hu, da kam das vierfüßige Gethier dahergerennt mit Gebraus, daß die Erde zitterte;
sentences.l: When the day broke, when the battle was to be delivered hu, then came the four-footed beast-kind running along with a roar, so that the earth trembled;
sentences.i: When the day broke on which the battle was to be fought — hu — the four-footed beasts came running up with such a roar that the earth trembled;
sentences.n: The 1857 text really does print a bare “hu” here, mid-sentence and before the comma; it is not a slip of this edition’s transcription and it is left exactly as printed. It reads as the narrator’s indrawn breath before the battle. “eine Schlacht liefern” is the set phrase for giving battle.

sentences.t: Zaunkönig mit seiner Armee kam auch durch die Luft daher, die schnurrte, schrie und schwärmte daß einem angst und bange ward;
sentences.l: Wren with his army came along through the air too, which whirred, shrieked and swarmed so that one became anxious and afraid;
sentences.i: The wren too came on through the air with his army, which whirred and shrieked and swarmed until one grew frightened and sick at heart;
sentences.n: Impersonal again: “einem … ward angst und bange”, with the person in the dative “einem”, one — the fear comes upon you rather than being felt by you. “angst und bange” is a fixed pair.

sentences.t: und giengen sie da von beiden Seiten an einander.
sentences.l: and went they there from both sides at one another.
sentences.i: and so they went at one another from both sides.
sentences.n: “an einander gehen” — to go at each other, to join battle.

sentences.t: Der Zaunkönig aber schickte die Hornisse hinab, sie sollte sich dem Fuchs unter den Schwanz setzen und aus Leibeskräften stechen.
sentences.l: The wren however sent the hornet down, she was to set herself under the fox’s tail and sting with all bodily strength.
sentences.i: But the wren sent the hornet down: she was to settle under the fox’s tail and sting with all her might.
sentences.n: “dem Fuchs unter den Schwanz” is the dative of possession — under *the fox’s* tail; German much prefers this to a possessive. “aus Leibeskräften” — with all the strength of the body.

sentences.t: Wie nun der Fuchs den ersten Stich bekam, zuckte er, daß er das eine Bein aufhob, doch ertrug ers und hielt den Schwanz noch in der Höhe:
sentences.l: When now the fox got the first sting, he twitched, so that he lifted the one leg up, yet he bore it and held the tail still up in the height:
sentences.i: When the fox got the first sting he twitched, so that he lifted one leg; but he bore it and still held his tail up:
sentences.n: “ers” is “er es” run together, as speech does. “ertrug” is from “ertragen”, to endure.

sentences.t: beim zweiten Stich mußt er ihn einen Augenblick herunter lassen:
sentences.l: at the second sting he had to let it down a moment:
sentences.i: at the second sting he had to let it down for a moment:
sentences.n: “mußt” stands here for “mußte”, had to, clipped short; the ß is the 1857 spelling.

sentences.t: beim dritten aber konnte er sich nicht mehr halten, schrie und nahm den Schwanz zwischen die Beine.
sentences.l: at the third however could he hold himself no longer, cried out and took the tail between the legs.
sentences.i: but at the third he could hold out no longer: he cried out and put his tail between his legs.
sentences.n: “sich halten” — to hold out, keep one’s composure. The tail between the legs means in German what it means in English.

sentences.t: Wie das die Thiere sahen, meinten sie alles wäre verloren und fiengen an zu laufen, jeder in seine Höhle:
sentences.l: When the animals saw that, they thought everything was lost and began to run, each into his den:
sentences.i: When the beasts saw that they thought all was lost and began to run, each into his own den:
sentences.n: “Thiere” is the 1857 spelling of Tiere. “fiengen an” is “anfangen”, to begin, with the particle in front (modern fingen an); “wäre” marks the thought as reported.

sentences.t: und hatten die Vögel die Schlacht gewonnen.
sentences.l: and had the birds won the battle.
sentences.i: and so the birds had won the battle.
sentences.n: The verb-first opening carries the previous sentence on rather than starting fresh — a narrative “and so”.

sentences.t: Da flog der Herr König und die Frau Königin heim zu ihren Kindern, und riefen „Kinder, seid fröhlich, eßt und trinkt nach Herzenslust, wir haben den Krieg gewonnen.“
sentences.l: Then flew the lord king and the lady queen home to their children, and called “Children, be merry, eat and drink to your heart’s desire, we have won the war.”
sentences.i: Then the king and queen flew home to their children and called, “Children, be merry, eat and drink to your hearts’ content: we have won the war.”
sentences.n: “nach Herzenslust” — as the heart desires. “eßt” is the 1857 spelling of esst, the plural imperative.

sentences.t: Die jungen Zaunkönige aber sagten „noch essen wir nicht, der Bär soll erst vors Nest kommen und Abbitte thun und soll sagen daß wir ehrliche Kinder sind.“
sentences.l: The young wrens however said “still we eat not, the bear shall first come before the nest and do apology and shall say that we are honourable children.”
sentences.i: But the young wrens said, “We are not eating yet: the bear must first come before the nest and beg pardon, and say that we are honest children.”
sentences.n: “Abbitte thun” — to make formal apology, a phrase from the old courts; “thun” is the 1857 spelling of tun. “vors” = vor das.

sentences.t: Da flog der Zaunkönig vor das Loch des Bären und rief „Brummbär, du sollst vor das Nest zu meinen Kindern gehen und Abbitte thun und sagen daß sie ehrliche Kinder sind,
sentences.l: Then flew the wren before the hole of the bear and called “Growl-bear, you shall go before the nest to my children and do apology and say that they are honourable children,
sentences.i: Then the wren flew to the mouth of the bear’s den and called, “Growl-bear, you are to go before the nest to my children and beg pardon and say that they are honest children,
sentences.n: “des Bären” is the genitive of a weak noun: “der Bär” takes -n in every case but the nominative.

sentences.t: sonst sollen dir die Rippen im Leib zertreten werden.“
sentences.l: otherwise shall to you the ribs in the body be trampled to pieces.”
sentences.i: or the ribs in your body shall be trampled to pieces.”
sentences.n: “dir … die Rippen” is once more the dative of possession: your ribs. “zertreten” — to trample apart.

sentences.t: Da kroch der Bär in der größten Angst hin und that Abbitte.
sentences.l: Then crept the bear thither in the greatest fear and did apology.
sentences.i: Then the bear crept there in the greatest fear and begged pardon.
sentences.n: “that” is the 1857 spelling of “tat”, the preterite of thun/tun.

sentences.t: Jetzt waren die jungen Zaunkönige erst zufrieden, setzten sich zusammen, aßen und tranken und machten sich lustig bis in die späte Nacht hinein.
sentences.l: Now were the young wrens first satisfied, set themselves together, ate and drank and made themselves merry until into the late night.
sentences.i: Only now were the young wrens satisfied; they sat down together, ate and drank and made merry far into the night.
sentences.n: “erst” here means “only then, not before”. “sich lustig machen” is to make merry — not the modern sense of making fun of someone.

glossary.angst: Angst — fear, dread (impersonal idiom: einem wird angst, fear comes upon one)
glossary.ausmachen: ausmachen — to settle, to have out (a quarrel); the modern sense “to put out, extinguish” is not this one
glossary.bange: bange — afraid, anxious (einem wird angst und bange: fear comes upon one)
glossary.bös: böse — angry, cross (short form bös; also: wicked, evil)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; also ‘he/she’ for neuter nouns such as das Kind, das Mädchen)
glossary.halte: halten — hold (1st sg. present, ich halte; also imperative halte!)
glossary.kehrten: umkehren — turned about, turned back (3rd pl. past; separable um-)
glossary.lauft: laufen — run! (2nd pl. imperative; the 3rd sg. is läuft)
glossary.los: los — off, straight at (in darauf los marschieren: to march straight at); also los sein: to be rid of
glossary.mußt: müssen — must (2nd sg. mußt; also clipped for mußte, had to)
glossary.müßt: müssen — must, have to (2nd pl. present; 1857 spelling of müsst)
